Keep what matters.

An order-adjustment concept inside Redshop checkout. It helps a buyer keep important product attributes while comparing the complete delivered cost.

Try the core experience

  1. Start with the two-item cart. Select Check out(2).
  2. Scroll inside the phone. The complete test total is $67.00. Open See order options.
  3. Review the suggested $50.50 floral-mug option and its explanation. No item is locked by default. Under Other ways to lower your total, select Keep my original mug to compare the $62.34 necklace-replacement option. Review, update, then Undo.
  4. Try “Still floral, and under $40.” Confirm the conditions and inspect the no-match recovery.
  5. Type or record your own request. Local AI proposes editable conditions; the catalogue and quote engine determine executable options.

AI and voice

Local Qwen runs through WebLLM on supported GPUs or Transformers.js on CPU/WASM, after a one-time model download. CPU interpretation can take tens of seconds. No API key or inference account is used. Voice becomes editable text through browser speech recognition, with local Whisper as a fallback. Browser speech services may process audio remotely. Transcripts remain editable.

If a model or device is unavailable, manual condition editing remains available and is explicitly labeled. It is not represented as AI output.

Recommendation and voice changes

After checking same-item quotes, the fixed default offers prioritize a floral mug with a lid, with lower-price and original-mug alternatives available. This is a deliberately bounded catalogue rule, not an inference that an expensive item matters less. Explicit lowest-price requests override this soft ranking; hard budgets and must-have conditions always filter first. This attribute rule is not a learned personalized recommender.

Browser speech ending without new words now produces a failure state and an on-device transcription button (except permission and microphone failures, which need resolution first). Local Whisper downloads a model on first use. Physical microphone transcription has not yet passed end-to-end verification.

Current demo scope

Two selected items and three replacement offers: two mugs and one necklace. Neither original item is locked by default. Explicit keep requirements protect the selected item; candidates change at most one item at a time. Keeping both items can produce no saving. The replacement necklace has no inherited original-shop coupon. The report separates the two-item demonstration from the proposed 1–3-item product scope. Session context favors floral attributes and can leave ranking unchanged; saved-original-cup context prioritizes keeping that cup. Both are transparent simulated rules, not a trained personalization model. The AI model reads text, while product visual attributes are catalogue fixtures.

Check personalization

Reset, open order options, then change Information available to “Saved this original cup.” The necklace replacement moves first. Set a total budget under $55: the floral mug becomes eligible while the necklace option exceeds budget. Ignoring browsing preferences restores the cart-only ranking. No inference becomes a protected item without your confirmation.

Evidence boundary

Original-product photographs and visual references come from supplied Redshop screenshots. The blue daisy mug and daisy necklace are fictional SKUs with labeled AI-generated illustrations. All quotes, availability, alternate offers and history signals are controlled demonstration data. No real account, payment or Redshop backend is accessed. The current language-model integration reads text; it does not infer properties from product photos.

Test status: Real local inference and 38 decision-engine checks were exercised. Small-model interpretation remains fallible; check the proposed conditions. Physical microphone-to-transcript verification remains pending because the test environment has no microphone.
